How lead II sees the heart

The rule: when the heart’s arrow points towards a lead’s positive end, that lead’s trace goes up; when it points away, the trace goes down; when it points across the lead, the trace stays near the line. The lead’s voltage is the arrow’s shadow on the lead’s direction (white dot).

How close to real children?

  • From data The twelve lead waves, the heart arrow and its loops, and the P, PR, QRS and QT times: the Heartverse simulator, fitted to the ECGs of children aged 1–14 whose ECGs were read as normal (one hospital).
  • Drawn for teaching The conduction path and where it sits, the order the glow spreads over the heart (the human sequence of Durrer 1970), and the heart’s shape and size (an adult atlas heart refitted to the child).

        HOW IT WORKS

        What this lab shows, and how sure it is

        1 · How a heartbeat works

        The heartbeat comes from the Heartverse Stage 2 simulator, fitted to the 12-lead ECGs of children aged 1–14 whose ECGs were read as normal (ZZU paediatric ECG database, one hospital). For each age and sex the page shows the typical child: every simulator setting at its average for that age, and the P, PR, QRS and QT times at the middle (50th centile) of the Stage 1 age profiles ( children). Changing the heart rate moves the QT along the QT–heart-rate relation measured in the same children.

        The simulator builds the beat from a heart vector: one arrow that sums the heart’s electrical activity at each moment. Each ECG lead records the arrow’s shadow on that lead’s direction, so twelve leads are twelve views of one arrow. The lead directions are the simulator’s own, fitted to the children; limb-lead directions come out close to the textbook ones and the page shows both.

        Drawn for teaching, not measured: the conduction path (sinus node, AV node, His bundle, bundle branches) and its position, the order the glow spreads over the heart muscle (the human sequence of Durrer et al., 1970), and the heart itself (an adult atlas heart refitted to the child). The glow’s timing follows the child’s own P wave, QRS and T wave.

        Two set values, not measured in children: the spark takes 35 ms to run down the His bundle and bundle branches before the QRS (in 64 adults the average was about 44 ms), and the heart starts to squeeze 30 ms after the QRS begins (about when the R wave peaks). How much the heart shrinks through the beat follows a released cardiac-cycle animation. These change only the animation, not the ECG.

        The explanations say only what their sources say, and every card carries numbered references: the conduction system and the waves, the order inside the ventricles, electrode positions, the limb leads, and the paper scale.

        2 · Growing up

        Shaded bands are the Heartverse Stage 1 age profiles: centiles by age and sex from children whose ECGs were read as normal at one hospital (ZZU), measured with the same software throughout. Points are published normal values: Rijnbeek et al. 2001 (healthy Dutch children) and Saarel et al. 2018 (Pediatric Heart Network, North America), median with 2nd–98th centile where reported. The sources used different machines and measuring methods, so their numbers differ; seeing the spread is part of the lesson.

        Each “why” note carries its references, mostly Dickinson 2005, and says only what they say; where the sources give no reason (heart rate), the note says so. All sources compare different children at different ages; none follows the same children as they grow.

        3 · QT readings

        The QT interval gets shorter as the heart beats faster, so it is “corrected” to a standard heart rate before it is compared with a limit such as 440 ms, the borderline upper limit of normal in children. Bazett’s formula is the standard one for children’s ECGs, and at fast heart rates it gives artificially long values, so a normal child can be flagged as having a long QT.

        For the chosen age and sex, the true QT is the typical (50th centile) or upper-normal (90th centile) QT of children of that age, from the Stage 1 age profiles. Changing the heart rate moves the QT along the QT–heart-rate relation measured in the same children for that age group; its exponent falls from about at ages 1–2 to at ages 10–14. The same QT is then corrected three ways:

        • Bazett · QTc = QT / RR1/2
        • Fridericia · QTc = QT / RR1/3
        • Age-adaptive (Haq et al., 2025) · QTc = QT + 0.75·x0.12·(HR + 10.8·ln x − 154), with x the age in weeks. It corrects to the usual heart rate for the age, not to 60 bpm, so the 440 ms line does not apply to it.

        Drift is how far each formula moves when only the heart rate changes for the same child. A perfect correction would not move. Drift is measured against this simulator’s own QT–heart-rate rule, so it shows that the formulas disagree, not which one is right.

        The 3D figure

        The body shape is MakeHuman’s base body, generated at 1, 10 and 14 years and blended for the ages in between, scaled to the WHO median height for the age (girls and boys averaged). The heart, lungs, liver, airway, abdominal organs and the vessels of the trunk come from the Human Reference Atlas (one adult man) and are refitted to each child, so their sizes and positions are illustrative, not paediatric measurements. The atlas has no arm or leg vessels; the main ones are drawn along the child’s joints following their textbook courses. The heart’s squeeze follows a released cardiac-cycle animation. In the QT readings section the heart close-up uses a detailed cutaway model.

        Limits

        • All ECG data come from one hospital and one ECG machine (ZZU, China). Published values from other countries are shown alongside for that reason.
        • Only of the children are aged 1–2 years. At these ages the typical child’s QT is short and its PR long compared with real children of the same age; the page says so where it matters.
        • Age data compare different children at different ages rather than following children as they grow.
        • Nobody’s true QT is known in real recordings, so the real-children figures show disagreement between formulas, not errors.
        • This page is for research and teaching. It does not diagnose anyone and must not be used for clinical decisions.
